expectations.text: Orders the fixes by efficiency - impact bought per unit of fix effort - not by raw severity and not purely by cheapness
expectations.evidence: The table carries explicit Impact and Effort columns and the ordering (1: counting method, High/near-zero; 2: internal filter, Medium/near-zero; 3: tag trigger, Critical/~1h) is justified in a dedicated paragraph: 'settings-class toggles (1, 2) clear before trigger corrections (3) even though (3) is more severe — same near-zero effort tier goes first, then the one-hour fix... 1 before 2 by impact (High beats Medium) within the same near-zero tier.' That is explicitly not raw-severity order (Critical is placed last, and the answer says so), and not pure cheapness either, since impact is the tie

expectations.text: Orders the fixes by efficiency - impact bought per unit of fix effort - not by raw severity and not purely by cheapness
expectations.evidence: The ordering is explicitly effort-vs-impact reasoned, not severity-ranked and not merely cheapest-first. Each item carries an effort tag ('No developer needed. 2 minutes', 'No developer needed (GTM)', 'likely needs the unavailable developer'), and the dedicated section 'Why this order, not severity order alone' states the logic: the near-free circuit breakers (0 and 1) come first because they are 'near-free and should be done in the same sitting to stop the bleeding immediately', while the single most damaging bug (item 2, the All-Pages trigger) is still placed on Day 1-2 rather than deferred
